job: Fresh graduate in business, finance and accounting
name: Nora Santos

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for talking with me. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. What you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. Tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm on the graduate buying team at Marlow Foods, a food distributor in Leicester that supplies cafes and school kitchens. I've been there since September. My day is chasing quotes from suppliers, updating the price sheet, and ringing round when a delivery of tomatoes doesn't show. I rent a room in a house with two nurses, and we mostly live on pasta.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like, and what's the hard part?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the haggling. There's a moment when a supplier drops five pence a kilo and you feel like you've done something real. The hard part is when a delivery goes wrong and everyone shouts at me even though it's not my fault. My dad's an electrician and my mum runs a market stall, and they've said I can always come home, so I'm not scared about money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it was always going to be a bit of both, some use and some hype. At work I'd say the tools are fine for drafting emails to suppliers and not much else. I'd tell friends we shouldn't be surprised the big promises fell short.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means my job stays pretty much as it is, which suits me. I'm learning from my manager Hamid, who's been buying for twenty years. Leicester has plenty of food businesses, and I've got over six months saved, so I'm not worried.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going: learn the supplier list, take my procurement certificate in the spring, and carry on with the little AI helper for emails. I'd save £400 a month. And I'd probably start thinking about a deposit for somewhere to live, but not yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, I think. Maybe a bit flat because nothing's changing, but flat is okay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you use AI for now, and how much do you trust it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I use it to draft emails and to tidy messy price lists from suppliers who send photos of handwritten sheets. I trust it about eighty percent, and I always read the numbers twice, because one wrong digit can cost us a pallet's worth of money. So it helps, but it doesn't replace me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would still keep you up at night in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Food prices, honestly. If prices keep going up, our customers like the school kitchens squeeze us harder, and Marlow might trim the team. That's not AI, that's just the market. It'd be on my mind every week even in the quiet picture.

say: I'd say it was always going to be a bit of **both**, some use and some hype.
I'd tell friends the tools are fine for **supplier emails**.
think: My job stays much as it is, and I'm learning from my manager **Hamid**.
Leicester has plenty of food businesses, so I'm not **worried**.
do: Learn the **supplier list** and take my procurement certificate in spring.
Start thinking about a **deposit**, but not yet.
feel: I feel **calm**, a bit flat, but flat is okay.
S0.quote: I trust it about eighty percent, and I always read the numbers twice, because one wrong digit can cost us a pallet's worth of money.
fieldNote: Nora is **steady** and secure, with a manager who teaches her.
She names **food prices** as her real pressure, not AI.
She uses AI for emails but **checks** numbers twice.

steps.text: Take my procurement certificate this spring
Keep using the AI helper for supplier emails
Save £400 a month toward a deposit

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's changing buying faster than people want to admit. I'd tell Hamid that we should test the new tools in a small way before the bosses force them on us. And I'd say to friends that it's not all bad, but not all good either.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, buying and quoting are on the list the card reads out, so I know the thinking part of my job is exposed. Chasing quotes and updating price sheets could be done by a tool in seconds. That means Marlow needs maybe half the buying team, and juniors are the easiest to cut.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd become the person who knows the suppliers, because relationships still need a human. I'd ask Hamid to bring me to supplier visits, and I'd learn the new tool before the rest of the team does. I'd also save more, £600 a month, and keep my CV fresh in case.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, a bit. Not terrified, but I'd check my phone for news every night.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Buying is on the card. Which of your jobs would software do first at Marlow?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The quote chasing, the price sheet updates and the reorder emails would go first. What stays is the haggling, the visits and the judgement about whether a supplier is going to let us down. Hamid's job would shift to managing the tool and the suppliers, and I'd want to be learning that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Hamid's job look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hamid would probably be fine, he knows everyone and has twenty years of trust. I'd be the one with less to show. The chance I have is that I'm cheap to keep and quick to learn, which counts for something in a small firm.

say: I'd say it's changing buying **faster** than people admit.
I'd tell Hamid to **test** the tools in a small way first.
think: Privately, quoting and price sheets are the **thinking part** of my job, and exposed.
Marlow may need half the buying team, and **juniors** are easiest to cut.
do: Become the person who knows the **suppliers**, since relationships need a human.
Ask Hamid to bring me to **supplier visits**.
Save **£600** a month and keep my CV fresh.
feel: I feel **anxious**, checking my phone for news every night.
S1.quote: The chance I have is that I'm cheap to keep and quick to learn, which counts for something in a small firm.
fieldNote: Nora recognises her tasks on the **card**, and says so.
Her plan: become the **relationship** person, close to Hamid.
Being **cheap and quick** is her honest edge.

steps.text: Learn the new buying tool before the rest of the team
Ask Hamid to take me on supplier visits
Keep my CV fresh and talk to a recruiter

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's moving too fast, and governments need to catch up. At work I'd say we should be open about our plans, because the worst thing is silence. I'd probably say it a bit loudly to friends too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think it's the end of buying as a graduate job. A tool that does all the thinking can quote, haggle and book, and it can do it for pennies. The robots three years later would move the pallets, so the food business changes in both halves. I'd be twenty-four and starting from scratch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd save as much as I can, probably £800 a month, and cut back on takeaways and trips. I'd ask my parents what the stall and the electrical work look like in this world, because their jobs are more hands-on. And I'd look for work that still has people in it, like supplier relationships or retail.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared, but I'd try to keep it together. I wouldn't tell my housemates for a few days, because I'd want to think it through first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Two years is quick. What changes in your daily life?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them plainly, and I'd say I might need to come home for a while. My mum would say we'll manage, which she says about everything. My dad would worry about the stock, because trades get hit later, and he'd be right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your parents?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The speed is the problem, because nobody has time to retrain at the same time. Hamid and I would both be scrambling. I'd rather be someone who moved early than someone who waited for a letter from HR.

say: I'd say it's moving **too fast**, and governments must catch up.
I'd ask my firm to be **open** about plans, because silence is worst.
think: Privately, it's the end of buying as a **graduate job**, and I'd start again at twenty-four.
Hands-on robots later affect the **pallets**, so the food business changes twice.
do: Save **£800** a month and cut takeaways and trips.
Ask my parents how their **hands-on** work looks in this world.
Look for jobs with **people** in them, like supplier relationships or retail.
feel: I feel **scared**, but I'd try to keep it together.
S2.quote: I'd rather be someone who moved early than someone who waited for a letter from HR.
fieldNote: Nora expects the job to go but still sees **cheap options** at home.
She asks her **parents** a practical question, whose trades hold on longer.
Her stance is to **move early**, which fits a steady adopter.

steps.text: Save £800 a month while I still have pay
Ask my parents if I can move home for a while
Apply for supplier-relationship and retail roles

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, we've got time to prepare, so let's do it. I'd say the firm should plan for training, and that people should push their MPs on retraining money. I'd mention it at work and at my parents' table.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd have a few good years, enough to move up from junior. By 2031 I'd be twenty-seven, maybe a category buyer with a small team. But I'd expect the job to be smaller or different by then, so I'd treat it as a stepping stone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish my procurement qualification, then look at moving into a field that needs a licence and a person, like food safety and compliance. I'd use the AI tools more every month so they're second nature. I'd also save £700 a month and think about a flat in two years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Okay, a bit anxious but manageable. It's a bit like a slow-moving tide.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Five years is more breathing room. What do you do differently?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask what I'm actually good at, which is dealing with people and smoothing things over. I'd pick the courses that build that, and I'd skip the ones that are just buttons to press. I'd ask Hamid, because he'll tell me straight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How do you decide what to learn?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The thing I'd change from the two-year picture is I wouldn't rush. In two years I'd grab anything. In five years I can choose the thing I actually want, and I'm more likely to stick with it.

say: I'd say we have time, so firms should plan **training** now.
I'd tell people to push their MPs for **retraining money**.
think: I'd get a few good years, enough to move up to **category buyer**.
By 2031 the job may be **smaller**, so it's a stepping stone.
do: Finish my **procurement** qualification, then look at food safety and compliance.
Use the AI tools more every month until they're **second nature**.
Save **£700** a month and think about a flat in two years.
feel: I feel **okay**, anxious but manageable, like a slow tide.
S3.quote: In two years I'd grab anything. In five years I can choose the thing I actually want, and I'm more likely to stick with it.
fieldNote: Nora separates **grabbing** from choosing, the key effect of more time.
She picks **people-facing** compliance work as her next step.
Hamid is her **sounding board**, which is why he's named so often.

steps.text: Use AI tools a little more every month
Save £700 a month toward a flat
Write to my MP about retraining money

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a long runway and we should use it carefully. I'd say schools should teach how to work with AI, and firms should plan for retraining. I'd say it calmly, because it doesn't feel urgent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's mostly fine for me. By 2036 I'd be thirty-two, with ten years in food and supply, maybe running a team. I'd have to change what I do twice, but I could handle that with ten years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay at Marlow while I learn, move up, and use the AI tools every week. I'd save for a flat in four years and put some into a pension from now. I'd also take a course every year, something that builds a skill the tools can't do easily.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty calm. I'd think about it now and then but I wouldn't lose sleep.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Ten years is long. What do you want to be doing by then?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want to be running a buying or planning team, and have a flat in Leicester. I'd want a partner and maybe a baby by thirty. I'd want a job where I decide things, rather than a tool deciding for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What worries you even in this slower picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Prices and housing, honestly, more than the machines. Even without AI, rents and food go up. If AI takes jobs, those worries get worse. So I'd say the real fear is a gap between what things cost and what people earn.

say: I'd say it's a **long runway** and we should use it carefully.
I'd say schools should teach people to **work with AI**.
think: It's mostly fine for me, with ten years in **food and supply** by 2036.
I would have to change what I do **twice**, but ten years is enough.
do: Stay at Marlow, move up, and use the **AI tools** every week.
Save for a **flat** in four years and start a pension now.
Take a **course** every year that builds a skill tools do poorly.
feel: I feel **pretty calm**, and wouldn't lose sleep.
S4.quote: I'd want a job where I decide things, rather than a tool deciding for me.
fieldNote: Ten years lets Nora think about **family**, flat and a team.
Her real fear is **prices and housing**, a gap between cost and pay.
She wants **decision-making** work, which sums up her goal.

steps.text: Stay at Marlow and aim for a team lead job
Save for a Leicester flat within four years
Take one new skills course each year
Plan for a partner and a baby by thirty

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year picture, because nobody would have time to retrain, including Hamid. What would help is honest information from firms, paid training, and something to catch people in between jobs, like income support. Housing support too, because rent is the bit that stays the same.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Just that I think my generation is going to be the guinea pigs. We were told to get a degree, and now the jobs that the degree was for might not exist. I'm not angry, exactly, but I'd like someone to say sorry.

headlineQuote: We were told to get a degree, and now the jobs that the degree was for might not exist.
portrait: Nora, 22, is a **graduate buyer** at a food distributor in Leicester, and uses AI for emails now and then.
Her mum runs a market stall and her dad is an electrician, so she has a **safe place** to land.
She sees quoting and price sheets as the first tasks to go, and plans to become the **supplier relationship** person.
She is calm when little changes, anxious in the fast pictures, and wants honesty from **firms and government**.
biggestWorry: The **two-year** picture, because nobody would have time to retrain, including her manager Hamid.
whatWouldHelp: Honest information from firms and paid **training**.
Income support between jobs, plus **housing** support.
